title: What Can a 2-Year-Old Usually Do? A Simple At-Home Checklist
label: Development Checklists
desc: A plain-language checklist of the motor, play, and self-care skills many 2-year-olds are working on, plus easy ways to practice at home.
html:
Two is a busy age. Kids go from wobbly walkers to little climbers in a matter of months, and parents often wonder whether their child is "on track."

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, gets this question a lot. Her answer is always the same:

"Look at the overall picture, not one skill. Every child has a few things that come later."

Here is a simple checklist she shares with parents.

Common skills around age 2

Big movement

  • Runs, even if a little stiffly
  • Climbs onto the couch or a low chair
  • Kicks a large ball forward
  • Walks up stairs while holding a hand or the rail

Hands

  • Stacks 4 to 6 blocks
  • Scribbles with a crayon, often with a fist grip
  • Turns pages of a board book, sometimes a few at a time

Self-care

  • Uses a spoon, with plenty of spills
  • Drinks from a cup with a little help
  • Helps pull off socks or a hat

Play

  • Pretends to feed a doll or stuffed animal
  • Copies what grown-ups do, like sweeping or talking on the phone

Easy ways to practice

  • Practice stairs together, one step at a time
  • Tape big paper to the table so it doesn't slide while they scribble
  • Let them pour water from cup to cup during bath time
  • Set up a pretend tea party with real cups and spoons

None of this needs special toys. Everyday routines are the best practice.

When to check in with a professional

  • Your child isn't walking by 18 months
  • They lose skills they used to have
  • They show little interest in people or play
  • Most of the list feels far away, not just one or two items

Final thoughts

A checklist is a guide, not a test. If your child loves one area and is slower in another, that's very common at two.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Heavy Work for Kids: 8 Indoor Activities That Help Busy Bodies Calm Down
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Pushing, pulling, and carrying give kids strong body input that often helps them settle. Here are 8 easy heavy work activities to try at home.
html:
Some kids seem to bounce off the walls, especially in winter when they can't run around outside. My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, often suggests something called "heavy work."

"Heavy work means using your muscles against resistance. Pushing, pulling, carrying. It gives the body strong input, and many kids feel calmer afterward."

The body sense behind this is called proprioception. It tells us where our body is and how much force we're using. Kids who crash, jump, or squeeze hard are often looking for more of it.

8 heavy work ideas

Push a laundry basket

Fill a basket with a few books and let your child push it across the room. It turns into a race very quickly.

Carry groceries

One light bag from the car to the kitchen is real, useful work. Kids love being trusted with a job.

Wall push-ups

Hands on the wall, lean in, push back. Count to ten together.

Tug of war with a towel

Sit on the floor facing each other and pull. Keep it gentle and let them win sometimes.

Animal walks

Bear crawls and crab walks put weight through the arms and shoulders.

Pillow sandwich

Your child lies between two couch cushions and you press gently on the top one. Many kids ask for "more."

Move the chairs

Before dinner, let them help push chairs to the table.

Play dough

Squishing, rolling, and pulling dough works the small muscles of the hands.

When to use heavy work

  • Before tasks that need focus, like homework or meals
  • After school or daycare, when kids come home wound up
  • Before bed, as part of winding down

Final thoughts

Heavy work isn't a cure for every busy day, but it's an easy tool to try. Five minutes of pushing and pulling can change the whole evening.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: An OT's Gift Guide: Toys That Build Skills, Age by Age
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Looking for gifts that are fun and build real skills? A pediatric OT's simple guide to toy types for ages 1 to 6, plus what to skip.
html:
Every December, relatives ask what to buy. My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, has a simple rule:

"The best toys make the child do the work, not the toy."

Here is her age-by-age guide to toy types. No brand names needed.

Toy types by age

Age 1

  • Stacking cups and rings
  • Push toys for new walkers
  • Board books with thick pages

Age 2

  • Chunky wooden puzzles with knobs
  • Big crayons and washable paint
  • Shape sorters

Ages 3 to 4

  • Play dough and simple tools
  • Lacing cards and big beads
  • Kid scissors with a few cutting strips

Ages 5 to 6

  • Building sets with small pieces
  • Simple board and card games
  • Craft kits they can finish on their own

What to look for

Open-ended

A set of blocks can be a tower, a road, or a zoo. Toys with one "right" way get boring quickly.

Hands do the work

If the toy lights up and talks while the child just presses a button, the hands aren't learning much.

Just a bit hard

A toy that's slightly challenging keeps kids interested. Too hard and it ends up in the closet.

Grows with them

Blocks, art supplies, and balls stay useful for years.

What to skip

  • Toys with many tiny pieces for kids under 3
  • Too many gifts at once (it's hard to focus on any of them)

Final thoughts

A simple toy that gets played with every day beats a flashy one that's forgotten by New Year's.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: How to Teach a Toddler to Blow Their Nose (Just in Time for Cold Season)
label: Daily Routines
desc: Nose blowing is a surprisingly tricky skill. Here are simple breathing games and step-by-step tips to help toddlers and preschoolers learn it.
html:
Cold season is here, and many parents are trying to teach their little ones to blow their nose. It's harder than it looks.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, explains why:

"Kids have to close their mouth and push air out through the nose on purpose. Most toddlers have never done that."

So the first step isn't the tissue. It's breathing games.

Breathing games first

Fog up a mirror

Show your child how to keep their mouth closed and breathe out through the nose onto a mirror. Seeing the fog makes it click.

Blow a cotton ball

Put a cotton ball on the table and try to move it with air from the nose only.

Smell the flower

Practice breathing in through the nose, slowly. This helps kids notice their nose is for air, too.

Feather race

Take turns blowing a feather across the table. Use the mouth first, then try the nose.

Nose blowing steps

1. Close the mouth and press the lips together

2. Gently hold one side of the nose

3. Blow out through the nose, like a small puff

4. Wipe, wash hands, and praise the effort

Many kids blow in instead of out at first. That's normal. Go back to the mirror game and try again another day.

Tips that help

  • Practice when your child is healthy, not mid-cold
  • Let them practice in front of a mirror
  • Use soft tissues so it doesn't hurt
  • Show them how you do it, slowly

Final thoughts

Most kids learn somewhere between 2 and 4 years old. A few minutes of breathing games each day makes it much easier.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Hair Washing Meltdowns: Why Some Kids Hate It and What Helps
label: Daily Routines
desc: If hair washing ends in tears, sensory reasons may be part of it. Here's why some kids struggle and simple changes that make bath time easier.
html:
For some families, hair washing is the hardest part of the day. Lots of crying, lots of splashing, and everyone ends up wet.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, says it often isn't stubbornness.

"For some kids, hair washing is several hard sensations at once."

Why some kids struggle

Water on the face

Water running over the eyes and nose can feel scary, especially for kids who are sensitive to touch.

Tilting back

Leaning the head back can feel like falling. Kids whose balance system is sensitive may panic.

Scalp touch

Light, quick touch on the scalp can feel too strong, even ticklish or painful.

No control

The water comes when the grown-up decides. Not knowing when it's coming makes it worse.

What helps

Keep the eyes dry

A bath visor or a folded washcloth held over the eyes helps many kids.

Pour from a cup, slowly

Say "One, two, three, water!" before each pour. Predictable is calmer.

Use firm pressure

Firm scrubbing with the fingertips often feels better than light, quick rubbing.

Count together

"We'll rinse for ten. Let's count." A clear end makes it easier to hold on.

More ideas

  • Let your child hold the cup and pour some water themselves
  • Try washing hair sitting up instead of lying back
  • Practice "pouring" on a doll's hair first
  • Wash hair every other day if that's okay for your family

Final thoughts

It may take a few weeks, but small changes add up. Start with what bothers your child most and change that first.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Nail Trimming Without the Battle: OT Tips for Touch-Sensitive Kids
label: Daily Routines
desc: Some kids fight nail trimming because it feels strange or uncomfortable. Here are OT-inspired tips to make it calmer and quicker.
html:
Nail trimming can turn into a wrestling match. Kids pull their hands away, cry, or hide under the blanket.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, says some kids really do feel it more.

"The fingertips have lots of nerve endings. For touch-sensitive kids, the pressure and the click can feel strange."

The good news is that a bit of preparation helps.

Before trimming

Firm hand squeeze

Before you start, give each hand a firm squeeze and press on the palms. Deep pressure helps the hands feel calmer.

Trim after a bath

Nails are softer after a bath, so clipping is easier and quicker.

Show the clippers

Let your child hold the clippers (closed) and look at them. Unknown tools feel scarier.

Same spot each time

A regular place, like a certain chair, makes it feel like a routine.

During trimming

One finger at a time

Count each finger out loud. "Five more, four more..." A countdown helps.

Hold firmly

A firm, steady hold on the finger feels better than a light, hesitant touch.

Give them a job

Some kids do better holding a toy in the other hand or watching a short song.

End clearly

Finish with a high five or a favorite song so it ends on a good note.

If it's still hard

  • Trim a few nails today and a few tomorrow
  • Try a nail file instead of clippers for very sensitive kids
  • Trim while they're sleepy or relaxed

Final thoughts

It doesn't have to be all ten nails at once. Calm and short is better than complete and stressful.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Puzzle Skills by Age: From Knob Puzzles to 100 Pieces
label: Development Checklists
desc: Puzzles grow with your child. Here are the typical puzzle stages from age 1 to 6 and how to pick the right next puzzle.
html:
Puzzles look like simple toys, but they build a lot: hand control, visual skills, and patience. My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, likes puzzles because the difficulty is easy to adjust.

"The right puzzle is one step above what your child can already do. Not three steps."

Puzzle stages by age

Ages 1 to 2: knob puzzles

Wooden boards with 3 to 5 shapes and big knobs. Kids learn that a shape fits a matching hole, and the knob trains a pinch grip.

Ages 2 to 3: chunky puzzles

Thick pieces that make one picture, usually 4 to 6 pieces. Kids start turning pieces to make them fit.

Ages 3 to 4: first jigsaws

Puzzles with 12 to 24 pieces. Kids begin to notice edges and colors.

Ages 5 to 6: bigger jigsaws

48 to 100 pieces, often with some help. Kids can plan and use strategies.

These ages are rough. Many kids move faster or slower, and that's fine.

Puzzle tips

Edges first

Show your child how to find the straight-edge pieces first. It's their first real strategy.

Sort by color

Make piles of sky pieces, grass pieces, and so on.

Keep the picture visible

Put the box on the table so they can compare.

Stop before they're tired

Big puzzles can be finished over several days. Ending on a good note matters more than finishing.

Signs a puzzle is too hard

  • Your child gives up after a minute
  • They try to force pieces in
  • They ask you to do it

Go back one step and try the harder one again in a few weeks.

Final thoughts

Puzzles are one of the easiest ways to grow hand and visual skills at home. Choose the next step and let your child feel the "click" of success.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Snow Play Is Sensory Play: 7 Ideas Indoors and Out
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Snow gives kids cold, heavy, and crunchy input all at once. Here are 7 snow play ideas, including indoor options for very cold days.
html:
When it snows, kids rush to the window. My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, says snow is one of the best sensory toys there is.

"Snow is cold, heavy, crunchy, and changes shape. Kids get a lot of input without even thinking about it."

Outdoor snow play

Build a snowman

Rolling a big snowball is real heavy work for the arms, shoulders, and legs.

Snow angels

Moving arms and legs at the same time builds body awareness and coordination.

Shovel a path

A kid-size shovel turns a chore into a game. Pushing and lifting snow gives strong muscle input.

Footprint trails

Take turns making a path and following each other's footprints. It's great for balance.

Indoor snow play

On very cold days, bring the snow to your child.

Snow in a bin

Fill a plastic bin with snow and put it on a towel. Add cups and spoons.

Hide small toys

Bury small toys and let your child dig them out with their hands or a spoon.

Color the snow

A spray bottle with water and a drop of food coloring makes snow painting.

Watch it melt

Put a cup of snow by the window and check on it every few minutes.

For kids who dislike cold hands

  • Start with gloves and let them take one off when they're ready
  • Use tools first, then fingers
  • Keep warm water nearby to warm hands

Final thoughts

Snow is free, and it doesn't last. Next time it falls, let your child explore it with their whole body.

Dress kids warmly and keep outdoor play short in very cold weather.

title: From Sippy Cup to Open Cup: How to Teach Your Child to Drink From a Cup
label: Picky Eating & Mealtime
desc: Drinking from an open cup is an important mealtime skill. Here's when kids usually learn it and step-by-step tips with fewer spills.
html:
Many kids drink from sippy cups for a long time. They're convenient, but drinking from an open cup is a skill worth practicing.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, explains:

"An open cup asks the lips and jaw to work together to control the flow. It's good practice for the mouth muscles used in eating and speech."

Many babies can start trying an open cup with help around 6 to 12 months.

Open cup steps

Start with a tiny amount

Pour in just one or two sips. A little water means little mess.

Try a two-handled cup

Handles help kids hold the cup steady with both hands.

Choose a small cup

A small cup is easier to tip slowly.

Practice at every meal

A few sips at each meal is better than one big practice now and then.

Fewer spills

Practice in the bath

Spills don't matter in the tub, so everyone can relax.

Thicker drinks first

A thicker drink moves more slowly, so it's easier to control.

Show slow sips

Kids copy what they see. Drink slowly from your own cup next to them.

Set the cup down between sips

Teach "sip and set down." It helps them pace.

What to expect

  • Lots of spills at first. That's normal
  • Dribbling down the chin for a few weeks
  • Big improvement once it becomes a daily habit

Final thoughts

There's no need to throw away the sippy cup right away. Just add an open cup to meals and let practice do the rest.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Why Does My Child Hold Food in Their Mouth? Food Pocketing Explained
label: Picky Eating & Mealtime
desc: Some kids keep food in their cheeks for a long time instead of swallowing. Here are common reasons and gentle ways to help at mealtime.
html:
Some kids take a bite and then keep it in their cheek for minutes. Meals stretch on, and parents worry.

This is sometimes called "food pocketing." My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, says there are a few common reasons.

Common reasons

The food is hard to chew

Tough or mixed textures, like meat, can be hard for little jaws. Kids hold it because they don't know what to do next.

Less mouth awareness

Some kids don't feel food in their cheeks as clearly. They simply forget it's there.

Not hungry

If snacks or milk came shortly before the meal, there's little reason to keep eating.

Distracted

Screens and toys at the table pull attention away from chewing and swallowing.

What can help

Smaller bites

Small pieces are easier to chew and finish.

Softer textures first

Start with textures your child manages well, then slowly add tougher ones.

Crunchy foods

Crunchy foods give strong input that helps kids notice food in their mouth.

A calm table

No screens, fewer toys. Talk together instead.

Other tips

  • Keep meals to about 20 to 30 minutes
  • Leave at least two hours between snacks and meals
  • Gently remind: "Chew, chew, swallow"
  • Eat together so they can watch you chew

When to check in with a professional

  • Pocketing happens at almost every meal
  • Your child coughs or gags often while eating
  • They aren't growing as expected

Final thoughts

Most food pocketing improves with smaller bites and calmer meals. If it doesn't, a feeding specialist can help.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Spoon and Fork Skills by Age: What to Expect at the Table
label: Picky Eating & Mealtime
desc: Using a spoon and fork takes years to master. Here's what to expect from age 1 to 6 and simple ways to help your child feed themselves.
html:
Watching a toddler try to eat with a spoon can be messy. But it's an important skill, and it takes years to get smooth.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, reminds parents:

"Messy eating is practice. Every spill teaches the hand something."

Utensil skills by age

Around age 1

Holds a spoon and bangs it on the table. Mostly eats with fingers, and that's perfect.

Around age 2

Scoops with a spoon and gets some food in. Expect spills, especially with runny foods.

Around age 3

Uses a spoon fairly well and starts stabbing soft foods with a fork.

Ages 5 to 6

Begins using a kid-safe knife to spread or cut soft foods.

Helpful tips

Short, thick handles

Small hands control short, thick handles more easily than long, thin ones.

Start with sticky foods

Oatmeal, yogurt, and mashed potatoes stay on the spoon. Soup can wait.

Pre-load the spoon

Fill the spoon and hand it to your child. They get the feeling of success while they practice.

Use a bowl with high sides

Kids can push food against the side to scoop.

More tips

  • Sit your child with feet supported. A stable body helps the hands
  • Give them time. Rushing leads to more spills
  • Eat together and model how you use utensils

Final thoughts

The road from fingers to fork is long and messy. Put a towel under the chair and let your child keep practicing.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: How Long Should a Child Be Able to Focus? Attention Span by Age
label: Development Checklists
desc: Many parents worry their child can't sit still. Here are typical attention spans by age and simple ways to build focus at home.
html:
"My child can't sit still for more than five minutes!" It's one of the most common worries my wife hears as a pediatric occupational therapist.

Her first question is always: "How old is your child?" Because the answer might be completely normal.

Typical focus time by age

A common rule of thumb is about 2 to 3 minutes per year of age for a task chosen by an adult.

  • Age 2: about 4 to 6 minutes
  • Age 3: about 6 to 8 minutes
  • Age 4: about 8 to 12 minutes
  • Ages 5 to 6: about 10 to 15 minutes

Kids can focus much longer on things they love, like building with blocks. Tasks chosen by adults, like worksheets, are harder.

Building focus at home

Move first, then sit

A few minutes of jumping or heavy work before a quiet task helps many kids settle.

Clear the table

Too many things in view pull attention away. Put out one activity at a time.

Use a visible timer

"When the timer ends, you can play." A clear end makes it easier to stick with it.

Follow their interests

A child who loves trucks will practice counting much longer with toy trucks.

Signs to check in with a professional

  • Focus is much shorter than other kids the same age, in all settings
  • Your child can't finish even favorite activities
  • Teachers share the same concerns

Final thoughts

Kids' attention spans are shorter than many parents expect. Build focus slowly with movement breaks and activities they enjoy.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Holiday Travel With Kids: Sensory Tips for Long Car Rides and Flights
label: Daily Routines
desc: Long trips are hard on little bodies. Here are sensory-friendly tips for car rides and flights, plus a simple travel kit checklist.
html:
Holiday travel means sitting still for hours in a noisy, unfamiliar place. That's hard for adults, and even harder for little kids.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, suggests planning for the body, not just the luggage.

"Kids handle trips better when their bodies get what they need: movement, comfort, and something to do with their hands and mouth."

Before you go

Move a lot before the trip

Run, jump, or play at the park before getting in the car or going to the airport.

Show the plan

Use pictures or a simple list: car, airport, plane, Grandma's house. Knowing what's next lowers stress.

Pack comfort items

A familiar blanket or toy helps in new places.

Bring headphones

Airports and family gatherings can be loud. Headphones help sound-sensitive kids.

Travel kit ideas

  • Crunchy or chewy snacks: chewing can be calming
  • A water bottle with a straw
  • A busy bag with stickers, lacing cards, or a small notebook
  • A squeeze toy for busy hands

During the trip

Car rides

Stop every 1 to 2 hours. Let kids run, jump, or do wall push-ups at the rest stop.

Flights

Walk the aisle when it's allowed. Chewing or sipping during takeoff and landing may help with ear pressure.

When you arrive

  • Find a quiet corner your child can go to
  • Keep bedtime routines as similar as possible
  • Plan some downtime between big events

Final thoughts

A little planning for movement and comfort can make holiday travel much smoother for the whole family.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Let Them Wrap: Gift Wrapping Is Great Fine Motor Practice
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Cutting, folding, and taping wrapping paper builds real hand skills. Here's how to let kids help wrap gifts at every age.
html:
Gift wrapping season is here. Many parents wrap late at night after the kids are asleep, but my wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, suggests letting kids help.

"Wrapping is full of fine motor work: tearing tape, folding, cutting, holding things in place."

Wrapping jobs by age

Age 2: stickers

Let your child decorate wrapped gifts with stickers. Peeling stickers is great pinch practice.

Age 3: tape pieces

Tear off small pieces of tape and stick them along the table edge, ready to use.

Age 4: fold the ends

Show them how to fold the paper ends into triangles and press them flat.

Ages 5 to 6: cut along a line

Draw a line on the back of the paper and let them cut it with kid scissors.

Skills they practice

  • Tearing tape builds a strong fingertip pinch
  • Folding uses both hands together
  • Cutting builds scissor control
  • Tying ribbon (with help) practices finger coordination

Tips to keep it fun

  • Use small boxes. Square boxes are much easier than odd shapes
  • Choose thicker paper, which tears less
  • Use gift bags for the hard ones
  • Let go of perfect. The wrapping doesn't need to look neat

Final thoughts

Gifts wrapped by little hands look a bit messy, but they mean a lot. And the hands get stronger with every piece of tape.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Using Both Hands Together: A Bilateral Coordination Checklist
label: Development Checklists
desc: Bilateral coordination means using both hands together. Here is a simple checklist by age and everyday activities to build it.
html:
Many everyday tasks need both hands, each doing a different job. One hand holds the paper while the other cuts. One hand holds the jar while the other twists the lid.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, calls it teamwork between the hands.

"Bilateral coordination is a building block for writing, dressing, and eating."

Two-hand skills by age

Around age 1

Bangs two blocks together. Passes a toy from one hand to the other.

Around age 2

Holds a bowl with one hand while scooping with the other. Pulls apart large pop beads.

Around age 3

Strings large beads. Unscrews lids.

Ages 4 to 5

Cuts paper while the other hand holds and turns it. Buttons large buttons.

Activities to try

  • Opening and closing containers with twist lids
  • Rolling dough with both hands on a rolling pin
  • Clapping games like patty-cake
  • Ripping paper into strips
  • Pulling apart and pushing together building bricks

Signs to watch for

  • Your child almost always uses only one hand, and the other stays idle
  • They switch hands constantly when drawing past age 5
  • Tasks like dressing or cutting are much harder than for peers

Final thoughts

Every day is full of two-handed practice. Let your child open their own snacks and help in the kitchen, and their hands will learn to work as a team.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Holiday Cookie Decorating: Fine Motor Fun That's Also Food Play
label: Picky Eating & Mealtime
desc: Decorating cookies works small hand muscles and helps picky eaters get comfortable with food. Here's how to set it up by age.
html:
Holiday cookies are a tradition in many homes. My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, loves cookie decorating for two reasons.

"It's fine motor practice, and it's food play. Kids touch and smell food without pressure to eat it."

Hand skills in decorating

Sprinkles

Pinching a few sprinkles and dropping them in one spot is great fingertip practice.

Icing bags

Squeezing an icing bag builds hand strength. Small bags are easier for little hands.

Cookie cutters

Pressing a cutter into dough takes real force from the arms and hands.

Spreading

Spreading icing with a butter knife or spatula trains wrist control.

Jobs by age

  • Ages 2 to 3: sprinkles and cookie cutters
  • Ages 4 to 5: spreading icing with a dull knife
  • Ages 5 to 6: piping simple lines and dots
  • All ages: taste testing

A note for picky eaters

Kids who avoid new foods often feel safer when they touch and smell food first. Cookie decorating is a low-pressure way to get messy with food. You can try the same idea with fruit or vegetables later.

Tips for less mess

  • Put a baking tray under each cookie to catch sprinkles
  • Use small bowls for each topping
  • Give each child a few cookies, not a whole batch

Final thoughts

The cookies don't have to look pretty. Messy cookies made by small hands are some of the best holiday memories.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Teaching Kids to Wash Their Hands Properly (Without Daily Reminders)
label: Daily Routines
desc: Cold and flu season is a good time to teach real handwashing. Here are simple steps, songs, and visual tips that help kids do it on their own.
html:
Winter brings colds, and handwashing becomes extra important. But kids often splash water on their fingers for two seconds and call it done.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, suggests treating handwashing like any other skill.

"Break it into steps, make it easy to reach, and practice until it's automatic."

Handwashing steps

1. Wet hands with warm water

2. Use one pump of soap

3. Scrub for about 20 seconds: palms, backs of hands, between fingers, and fingertips

4. Rinse and dry with a towel

Making it stick

A step stool

If kids can't reach the sink comfortably, they rush. A sturdy stool makes it easier.

Picture steps by the sink

Draw or print four simple pictures and tape them at your child's eye level.

A short song

Singing a short song, like "Happy Birthday" twice, helps them scrub long enough.

Foam soap

Foam soap spreads easily and is fun to use.

For kids who dislike the feeling

Some kids don't like wet or slippery hands. Try:

  • Warm, not cool, water
  • Drying hands right away with a soft towel
  • Letting them control the faucet

Final thoughts

With a stool, a song, and a few pictures, most kids can wash their hands well on their own. Good habits now help all winter long.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Family Board Games by Age: What Kids Learn While They Play
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Holiday break is perfect for board games. Here's what type of game fits each age from 3 to 7 and the skills kids build along the way.
html:
Holiday break is a perfect time to bring out board games. My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, calls games "practice disguised as fun."

"Kids practice waiting, picking up small pieces, counting, and handling losing, all while they're having a good time."

Game types by age

Age 3: matching and memory

Simple memory card games with large pictures. Kids learn to wait for their turn and remember where things are.

Age 4: simple dice games

Roll the die, count the dots, and move that many spaces. It's early math and hand control in one.

Age 5: games with small pieces

Games that ask kids to pick up or stack small pieces with their fingers or tweezers are great fine motor work.

Ages 6 to 7: strategy and card games

Simple strategy games and card games where kids hold a hand of cards and plan ahead.

Skills from games

  • Taking turns and waiting
  • Picking up and placing small pieces
  • Counting spaces and comparing numbers
  • Handling losing and winning gracefully

Tips for young players

  • Keep games short. 10 to 15 minutes is plenty for preschoolers
  • Change the rules to make it easier if needed
  • Model being a good loser: "Oh no, I lost! Let's play again."
  • Let kids hold cards in a stand if their hands are small

Final thoughts

Board games give families time together and give kids real skill practice. Pick a game that fits your child's age and enjoy the holiday break.

title: Too Many New Toys? How Toy Rotation Helps Kids Play Longer
label: Daily Routines
desc: After the holidays, a pile of new toys can actually make kids play less. Here's how toy rotation works and how to set it up in one afternoon.
html:
After the holidays, many homes are suddenly full of new toys. Surprisingly, kids often play less, jumping from one toy to the next without settling.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, often recommends toy rotation.

"When there are fewer toys in view, kids play with each one longer and more creatively."

How to rotate toys

Sort into groups

Divide toys into 4 or 5 boxes.

Put out one group

Leave about 8 to 10 toys out at a time.

Store the rest out of sight

A closet or high shelf works well. If kids can see them, they'll ask.

Swap weekly

Every week or two, switch to the next box. Old toys feel new again.

A good mix in each group

Try to include one or two of each:

  • Building toys, like blocks
  • Pretend play, like dolls or a play kitchen
  • Hand toys, like puzzles or play dough
  • Movement toys, like a ball

Tips

  • Keep a few favorites out all the time
  • Let your child choose one toy to swap in early if they ask
  • Use clear, labeled bins so cleanup is easier
  • Donate toys that haven't been touched in several rotations

Final thoughts

Toy rotation takes one afternoon to set up and makes playtime calmer and longer. It's a great way to start the new year.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Block Building Stages: From Stacking to Making Whole Cities
label: Development Checklists
desc: Blocks grow with your child. Here are the common block building stages from age 1 to 6 and how to support each one.
html:
Blocks may be the oldest toy around, and my wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, still calls them one of the best.

"Blocks teach hand control, balance, planning, and problem solving. And kids never seem to outgrow them."

Block building stages

Around age 1: carrying and banging

Kids pick up blocks, carry them around, bang them together, and drop them in containers.

Around age 2: stacking

Simple towers, often knocked down right away. That's half the fun.

Around age 3: bridges and lines

Kids line blocks up like roads or trains and try to make bridges between two blocks.

Ages 4 to 6: scenes and stories

Kids build houses, zoos, and cities, then play stories in them.

How to support play

Plain blocks in different sizes

Simple wooden blocks leave room for imagination.

Build next to your child, not for them

Make your own tower nearby. Kids often copy new ideas.

Add props

Toy cars, animals, and people turn buildings into stories.

Talk about it

Use words like tall, short, wide, and balance. It builds early math language.

Signs to watch for

  • After age 2, your child shows no interest in stacking at all
  • Blocks always fall because their hands seem shaky or very stiff

Final thoughts

If your house is full of new toys after the holidays, don't put the blocks away. They might be the toy your child uses most next year.

title: Why Does My Child Keep Bumping Into Things? Body Awareness Explained
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Some kids bump into furniture, fall often, or use too much force. Here's how body awareness works and simple games to build it.
html:
Some kids seem to bump into everything: the table, the door frame, their siblings. Parents call them clumsy, but my wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, sees it differently.

"Many of these kids have a hard time feeling where their body is in space. It's called body awareness, and it can be practiced."

The sense behind body awareness comes from muscles and joints. It tells us how our arms and legs are positioned without looking.

Common signs

  • Bumps into furniture or people often
  • Pushes too hard: breaks crayons, hugs too tight
  • Falls more than other kids the same age
  • Leans on people or walls a lot

Body awareness games

Obstacle course

Use cushions, chairs, and blankets. Climb over, crawl under, squeeze through.

Simon says

"Touch your knees. Touch your elbows." Naming body parts while moving helps connect the two.

Wheelbarrow walk

You hold your child's legs while they walk on their hands. It's great heavy work for the arms.

Freeze dance

Dance to music and freeze when it stops. It trains body control.

Other everyday ideas

  • Carry heavier things, like a bag of books
  • Do animal walks around the house
  • Play in tight spaces, like a blanket fort

When to check in with a professional

  • Falls or injuries happen much more than with peers
  • Clumsiness gets in the way of play or school
  • It comes with other concerns, like trouble with handwriting or dressing

Final thoughts

Bumping into things isn't always just clumsiness. With movement games, many kids gain much better body awareness.

title: Thank-You Notes After the Holidays: Easy Writing Practice by Age
label: Development Checklists
desc: Thank-you notes are a meaningful way to practice writing. Here are realistic note-writing goals for ages 3 to 7 and tips to keep it short and fun.
html:
After the holidays, many families write thank-you notes. My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, sees it as a great writing opportunity.

"Kids are more motivated to write when the words are going to a real person."

The key is setting a goal that fits their age.

Note goals by age

Age 3: draw a picture

A picture of the gift or the person is a perfect thank-you.

Age 4: scribble their name

Add their name, or the first letter, under the picture.

Age 5: trace "Thank you"

Write "Thank you" lightly in highlighter and let them trace it.

Ages 6 to 7: write one sentence

"Thank you for the blocks. I love them." Spelling doesn't need to be perfect.

Keep it easy

One note a day

Writing ten notes at once is too much. One a day is easy.

Use small cards

Small cards mean less empty space to fill.

Fill-in-the-blank cards

"Thank you for the ____." Your child adds a word or a drawing.

Stickers at the end

Decorating is the reward for finishing.

Handwriting tips

  • Use short pencils or crayons for a better grip
  • Sit at a table with feet supported
  • Praise effort, not neatness

Final thoughts

A thank-you note is a short, meaningful writing task. Pick one goal that fits your child and send a little joy to someone they love.

title: How to Get Kids to Clean Up Their Toys (Without Yelling)
label: Daily Routines
desc: Cleaning up is a skill kids need to learn step by step. Here are age-based expectations and simple systems that make tidying easier.
html:
"Clean up your toys!" might be one of the most repeated phrases in any home with kids. And often the toys stay right where they are.

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, says cleanup is harder for kids than it looks.

"A messy room is too big a job. Kids need a smaller, clearer task."

What to expect by age

  • Age 2: puts a few toys in a bin when you show them
  • Age 3: cleans up with a grown-up helping
  • Age 4: sorts toys into labeled bins
  • Ages 5 to 6: cleans up one area on their own

Systems that help

Picture labels on every bin

A photo of cars on the car bin helps kids who can't read yet.

Small bins

Small, open bins are easier to fill than big chests with lids.

One job at a time

"Put all the cars in the car bin." Then the next job. Small steps are easier.

A cleanup song

The same song every time signals that it's cleanup time.

Other tips

  • Clean up together at first
  • Give a five-minute warning before cleanup
  • Keep fewer toys out (toy rotation helps a lot)
  • Praise the effort, not the result

Final thoughts

Cleanup is a skill, and it builds slowly. Make the job small and clear, and your child can do more than you might expect.

title: New Year, New Skills: Small Development Goals to Try in 2027
label: Development Checklists
desc: Instead of big resolutions, pick one small skill for your child to practice in the new year. Ideas by area from a pediatric OT.
html:
The new year is a time for goals, and that can include our kids, too. My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, suggests keeping it simple.

"Choose one small skill your child is almost ready for. Practice it a little every day, and you'll see real progress by spring."

Goal ideas by area

Self-care

  • Put on their own socks or shoes
  • Zip their own coat

Hands

  • Cut along a straight line
  • Draw a circle or a person

Mealtime

  • Use a fork for soft foods
  • Drink from an open cup

Routine

  • Wash hands alone
  • Help clean up toys

Making goals stick

Pick just one

One goal at a time is much easier than several.

Practice daily, briefly

Five minutes a day works better than an hour once a week.

Track progress

A simple sticker chart helps kids see how far they've come.

Celebrate small wins

"You did one sock all by yourself!" Small wins keep kids going.

How to choose the goal

  • Look for skills your child is already trying
  • Pick something that makes daily life easier
  • Make it fun, not a chore

Final thoughts

Thank you for reading OT Wife Notes this year. Here's to a new year full of small, happy steps for your family.
